generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, research ethics is not an afterthought but part of how the discipline defines good work. The British Psychological Society sets out standards that echo the ESRC principles: respect for participants, informed consent, protection from harm, and honesty about methods and findings. A psychology project that treats its ethics application as paperwork, rather than a design discipline, is weak however polished its write-up looks.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two psychology students preparing the same interview study on exam anxiety for ethical approval.

Tom treats the ethics application as a form to clear. The consent wording says nothing about how recordings will be stored, participation is described as expected of the module's students, and his link to the counselling service he is recruiting from goes unmentioned. The study may still gain approval, but it sits uneasily against the principles of informed participation, transparency and declared interest.

Amara reads her design against each principle in turn. Participation is made genuinely voluntary and informed, storage and responsibility are spelled out, and her link to the service is declared openly. Nothing about the study is hidden, so the application documents a design that is sound rather than merely permitted.

Both students will submit a form. Only Amara used the principles to improve the research itself, which is what treating ethics as integrity rather than paperwork means.
generatedProse.summary: Research ethics in psychology is the substance behind the ethics form, not the form itself. You can now justify ethical conduct as an expression of academic integrity, evaluate a psychology study against the six ESRC principles, and anticipate the issues an ethics application must address. The next lesson turns to the duties you take on once you start collecting data from participants.

check.body: A psychology study plans to recruit participants by telling them their seminar tutor expects them to take part. Which ESRC principle does this most clearly breach?

items.text: That participation should, wherever possible, be voluntary and appropriately informed.
That research should maximise benefit and minimise harm.
That lines of responsibility should be clearly defined.
That the independence of research should be maintained.

feedback.correct: That's right. Telling students a tutor expects participation makes it no longer freely voluntary.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Which principle is about the freedom to take part?
feedback.incorrectFinal: Recruiting through a tutor's expectation breaches voluntary, informed participation; the other principles are about outcomes, accountability and independence.
